title: Communication Services
summary: Communication is the process of sharing facts, ideas, opinions, thoughts and information through speech, writing, gestures or symbols between two or more persons — so it needs at least two persons. Elements of the communication process: sender (source — the person who sends the message), message (the subject matter — facts, ideas, feelings), medium or means (the channel that carries the message — letter, telephone, e-mail), receiver (the person who receives it) and feedback (the receiver's response directed back to the sender). The process is complete only when the receiver understands the message and gives feedback — e.g. drivers stopping at a red light, or a friend nodding.

Communication is to business what the bloodstream is to a person. It expresses facts, figures and ideas; helps control and coordinate departments and motivate employees; links the firm with suppliers and customers; helps the business run efficiently and builds a good public image; educates people and spreads knowledge of new products and techniques; and overcomes barriers of distance and language.

Verbal communication uses words: oral (spoken — talks, meetings, telephone, lectures) or written (letters, memos, circulars, notices, reports). Non-verbal communication: visual — pictures, graphs, symbols, diagrams (a traffic policeman showing a stop sign, a chart in class); aural — sounds such as bells, whistles, sirens (the school bell); gestural — body language (saluting the national flag, nodding, waving, a straight posture showing confidence). In an organisation, formal communication flows through officially prescribed channels; informal communication (the grapevine) flows through personal contacts. Nobody in an organisation can avoid communication.

Letters — written, low cost, keep a record. Telegrams — quick written messages charged by words (now discontinued in India). Telephone — instant oral contact; STD and ISD for distant calls; PABX for offices; mobile phones add SMS (short message service) and MMS. Telex — printed communication by teleprinters connected through an exchange. Fax (facsimile) — instantly sends an exact copy of handwritten or printed matter, diagrams and sketches over telephone lines. E-mail — messages, pictures and files sent instantly over the Internet. Voice mail — a computer system that records and stores telephone messages to be heard later. Teleconferencing — people in different places interact without sitting face to face: audio-conferencing (hear and respond from different locations) and video-conferencing (also see each other).

(1) Badly expressed message — poor words, wrong language, different interpretations (semantic barrier). (2) Screening or filtering — when a message passes through several levels, each person passes on only what suits him, so it gets distorted. (3) Inattention — people do not read notices or listen carefully. (4) Unclarified assumptions — sender and receiver assume different things. (5) Resistance to change — people ignore messages that disturb their routine. (6) Mutual distrust — lack of confidence between superior and subordinates. (7) Status and position — fear stops subordinates from speaking freely. (8) Complex organisation structure — long chains of command break messages down. Noise is any hurdle that disturbs communication.

vsa: Video-conferencing is a form of teleconferencing in which people at different places can hear and also see each other while talking, using cameras, screens and telecommunication or Internet links.

Teleconferencing is a system through which people interact without physically sitting together, using telephone, computers or television.
Audio-conferencing is two-way voice communication — participants at different places hear each other and respond immediately.
What is fax? State one advantage and one limitation.

Fax (facsimile) sends an exact copy of handwritten or printed matter, diagrams and sketches instantly over telephone lines.
Advantage: instant transmission over any distance.
Limitation: only documents of a standard size; the print may fade, so copies are kept.
State any two points of importance of communication in business.

(1) It coordinates departments, controls operations and motivates employees.
(2) It links the firm with suppliers and customers and builds a good public image.
sa: Explain the elements of the communication process.

(1) Sender — the person who starts communication and sends the message.
(2) Message — the subject matter: facts, ideas, feelings or information.
(3) Medium — the means that carries the message (letter, telephone, e-mail).
(4) Receiver — the person who receives the message.
(5) Feedback — the receiver's response directed back to the sender; it shows the message was understood.
What is meant by filtering in communication? How does it hinder effective communication?

Filtering (screening) means that when a message passes through several persons or levels, each one passes on only the part that gives a favourable impression and leaves out the rest.
It hinders communication because the message gets distorted and incomplete at each level, decisions are based on wrong information, and the top does not learn the real facts.

Fax: an electronic device that sends an exact copy of handwritten or printed documents, diagrams and sketches instantly over telephone lines to another fax machine.
Telex: printed communication using teleprinters connected through a central exchange; a message typed on one machine is automatically typed on the other.
la: Define communication. State the various elements in the communication process.

Communication is the process of sharing facts, ideas, opinions and information through speech, writing, gestures or symbols between two or more persons.
Elements: (1) Sender — the source who sends the message. (2) Message — the facts, ideas or feelings conveyed. (3) Medium — the means used (oral, written, telephone, e-mail). (4) Receiver — the person who gets the message. (5) Feedback — the receiver's response; the process is complete only when the receiver understands and responds.
'Communication is as necessary to business as the bloodstream is to a person.' Explain.

Just as blood carries oxygen to every part of the body, communication carries information to every part of a business.
(1) It conveys plans, orders and instructions to employees.
(2) It coordinates the work of departments and helps control operations.
(3) It motivates employees and builds good relations.
(4) It links the firm with customers, suppliers and government.
(5) It helps quick decisions and builds a good public image. Without it the business cannot function.
Explain any five barriers to effective communication.

(1) Badly expressed message — poor choice of words or language causes misunderstanding.
(2) Screening or filtering — the message gets distorted as it passes through levels.
(3) Inattention — people do not read or listen carefully.
(4) Unclarified assumptions — sender and receiver assume different things.
(5) Resistance to change — people ignore messages that disturb routine.
(6) Mutual distrust; status and position; complex organisation structure.
